# Method for Latency Measurement in Uplink and Downlink Packet Transmission

## Overview

This method provides a mechanism for measuring transmission latency in both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) directions within a communication network, enabling network entities and user equipment (UE) to accurately assess timing performance and take appropriate actions based on the measured results.

## Uplink Latency Measurement

The method enables a network entity to receive an uplink packet transmitted by a UE. This packet is received at the entity at a specific point in time, referred to as the **first time unit**. Critically, the packet itself contains embedded timing information—specifically, a **second time unit**—which indicates the exact moment at which the UE originally transmitted the packet.

Upon reception, the entity performs a latency calculation by determining the time difference between the first time unit (the reception timestamp at the entity) and the second time unit (the transmission timestamp recorded by the UE at the moment of sending). This difference represents the transmission latency experienced by the uplink packet as it traversed the network from the UE to the entity.

Once this latency value has been measured, the entity is configured to perform at least one corresponding action based on the result. Such actions may include, but are not limited to, adjusting scheduling parameters, triggering network optimization procedures, reporting the latency metric to other network functions, or modifying resource allocation strategies to improve future transmission performance.

## Downlink Latency Measurement

In a complementary manner, the method also supports latency measurement in the downlink direction. In this scenario, the UE receives a downlink packet transmitted by the network entity. Similar to the uplink case, this packet is received by the UE at a specific first time unit, and the packet contains a second time unit that marks the precise moment at which the entity transmitted the packet.

The UE then calculates the time difference between these two timestamps—the reception time at the UE and the transmission time recorded by the entity—thereby determining the downlink transmission latency.

## Latency Reporting

Following this measurement, the UE reports the calculated downlink latency information back to the entity. This feedback mechanism allows the entity to gain visibility into the actual end-to-end downlink transmission performance experienced by the UE, which may otherwise be difficult to observe directly at the network side.

## Significance

By enabling both uplink and downlink latency measurements—performed respectively by the entity and the UE—this method provides a comprehensive, bidirectional view of transmission timing performance across the communication link. This dual-direction visibility supports more informed decision-making for network optimization, quality-of-service management, and adaptive resource control strategies.

# Method for Latency Reporting in Packet Transmission Within Communication Networks

## Overview

This method provides a robust and efficient mechanism for measuring and reporting latency in packet transmission within modern communication networks, including but not limited to cellular, 5G, and next-generation wireless systems. The core innovation lies in embedding transmission time information directly within the packet itself, enabling precise, low-overhead latency calculations at the receiving entity without requiring complex synchronization protocols or external timestamping infrastructure.

## Detailed Description of the Method

### Packet Transmission and Timestamp Embedding

In this approach, a transmitting entity—which may be a network element (such as a base station, gNB, eNB, or core network function) or a User Equipment (UE)—embeds a timestamp corresponding to the transmission time unit directly into the packet payload or header prior to transmission. This transmission time unit represents the precise moment at which the packet departs the transmitting entity and enters the network for delivery to its intended recipient.

The embedding process can be implemented at various protocol layers, including but not limited to the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, Radio Link Control (RLC) layer, Packet Data Convergence Protocol (PDCP) layer, or even at higher application layers, depending on the granularity of latency measurement required and the specific network architecture in place.

### Reception and Latency Calculation

Upon receipt of the packet, the receiving entity—which may be a UE, network element, or intermediate node—extracts the embedded transmission timestamp from the packet. The receiving entity then records its own reception time, corresponding to the moment the packet is successfully received and processed.

The latency for that particular packet transmission is then calculated as the difference between the reception time and the embedded transmission time:

**Latency = Reception Time − Transmission Time**

This calculation can be performed in real-time or near-real-time, providing an accurate, per-packet measurement of the actual transmission delay experienced across the network path, including any propagation delay, processing delay, and queuing delay incurred during transmission.

### Bidirectional Latency Measurement

A key advantage of this method is its applicability to both uplink (UE-to-network) and downlink (network-to-UE) transmission scenarios:

- **Uplink Latency Measurement**: When a UE transmits a packet to a network entity, the UE embeds its transmission time unit into the packet. The network entity, upon reception, calculates the uplink latency by comparing its reception time against the embedded transmission timestamp from the UE.

- **Downlink Latency Measurement**: Conversely, when a network entity transmits a packet to a UE, the network entity embeds its transmission time unit into the packet. The UE, upon reception, calculates the downlink latency similarly.

This bidirectional capability ensures comprehensive latency visibility across both directions of communication, which is particularly valuable for applications requiring symmetric or asymmetric latency guarantees, such as Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) services, real-time gaming, industrial automation, autonomous vehicle communication, and other latency-sensitive applications.

### Latency Reporting Mechanism

Once the latency is calculated, the receiving entity may report this latency information back to a network entity, which could be a centralized network function, a management and orchestration system, or a network controller responsible for monitoring and optimizing network performance. This reporting can occur through several mechanisms:

1. **Periodic Reporting**: The receiving entity aggregates latency measurements over a defined time window and reports statistical summaries (e.g., average, minimum, maximum, or percentile-based latency values) to the network entity at regular intervals.

2. **Event-Triggered Reporting**: The receiving entity reports latency measurements immediately upon detecting that the calculated latency exceeds a predefined threshold, enabling rapid response to network degradation or Quality of Service (QoS) violations.

3. **On-Demand Reporting**: The network entity may explicitly request latency reports from the receiving entity for specific packets, flows, or time periods, allowing for targeted diagnostic or optimization purposes.

### Network Entity Actions Based on Latency Data

Upon receiving latency reports, the network entity can leverage this real-time or near-real-time latency data to perform a variety of network management and optimization actions, including:

- **Dynamic Resource Allocation**: Adjusting scheduling priorities, bandwidth allocation, or radio resource assignments to reduce latency for specific UEs or traffic flows experiencing degraded performance.

- **Handover Decision-Making**: Utilizing latency measurements as an additional metric, alongside signal strength and other quality indicators, to trigger handovers to alternative cells or access points that may offer improved latency performance.

- **Congestion Management**: Identifying network congestion points based on elevated latency reports and implementing congestion control mechanisms, such as traffic shaping, load balancing, or admission control adjustments.

- **QoS Enforcement**: Ensuring compliance with service-level agreements (SLAs) by dynamically adjusting network configurations to meet latency requirements specified for particular applications or service classes.

- **Network Slicing Optimization**: In network slicing architectures, using latency data to optimize resource allocation across different slices, ensuring that latency-sensitive slices receive appropriate prioritization.

- **Root Cause Analysis and Troubleshooting**: Aggregating latency data across multiple UEs, cells, or network segments to identify systemic issues, such as hardware bottlenecks, software inefficiencies, or backhaul limitations, that may be contributing to increased latency.

- **Predictive Analytics and Machine Learning Integration**: Feeding historical latency data into machine learning models to predict future network performance trends, enabling proactive network optimization and capacity planning.

### Advantages of the Method

This latency reporting method offers several significant advantages over traditional latency measurement techniques:

1. **Simplicity and Low Overhead**: By embedding the transmission timestamp directly within the packet, this method avoids the need for complex round-trip time (RTT) measurements, external synchronization protocols, or additional signaling overhead.

2. **Accuracy**: Since the transmission time is captured at the exact moment of packet departure and compared against the exact moment of reception, this method provides highly accurate, granular latency measurements at the packet level.

3. **Scalability**: This method can be applied across numerous packets, flows, and UEs simultaneously, providing a scalable solution for latency monitoring across large-scale networks with numerous concurrent users and services.

4. **Flexibility**: The method is agnostic to the specific network architecture and can be implemented across various generations of wireless technology, including 4G LTE, 5G NR, and future 6G networks, as well as in wired network environments.

5. **Real-Time Responsiveness**: The ability to calculate and report latency in real-time or near-real-time enables network entities to respond swiftly to changing network conditions, thereby improving overall Quality of Experience (QoE) for end users.

### Implementation Considerations

For successful implementation of this method, several technical considerations must be addressed:

- **Clock Synchronization**: While this method reduces reliance on complex synchronization protocols compared to RTT-based measurements, some degree of clock synchronization between the transmitting and receiving entities may still be necessary to ensure accurate latency calculations, particularly in scenarios involving strict timing requirements.

- **Timestamp Format and Precision**: The format and precision of the embedded timestamp (e.g., microsecond or nanosecond resolution) should be selected based on the specific latency requirements of the application or service being supported.

- **Packet Overhead**: Careful consideration should be given to the additional overhead introduced by embedding timestamp information within packets, balancing the need for accurate latency measurement against the impact on overall network efficiency and throughput.

- **Security and Integrity**: Mechanisms should be implemented to ensure the integrity and authenticity of embedded timestamps, preventing malicious manipulation that could lead to inaccurate latency reporting or network optimization decisions.

## Conclusion

This method represents a practical and effective solution for addressing the challenges of latency reporting in packet transmission within modern communication networks. By embedding transmission timestamps directly within packets and enabling straightforward latency calculations at the receiving entity, this approach facilitates accurate, real-time measurement and reporting of both uplink and downlink latencies. This, in turn, empowers network entities to make informed, data-driven decisions regarding resource allocation, QoS enforcement, and overall network performance management, ultimately contributing to enhanced user experience and more efficient network operation.

# Methods for Measuring: An Overview

Measuring is a fundamental process that underlies nearly every field of human endeavor, from scientific research to everyday practical tasks. The method chosen for measuring any given quantity significantly influences the accuracy, reliability, and usefulness of the results obtained.

## The Importance of Proper Methodology

The selection of an appropriate measuring method depends on several factors, including the nature of what is being measured, the required precision, available tools, and the context in which the measurement takes place. A method that works well for measuring length may be entirely unsuitable for measuring temperature, volume, or more abstract quantities like satisfaction or intelligence.

## Common Approaches to Measuring

**Direct Measurement**
This method involves comparing the object or quantity being measured directly against a standard unit. Using a ruler to measure length or a scale to measure weight are classic examples of direct measurement methods.

**Indirect Measurement**
Sometimes direct measurement isn't feasible, requiring indirect methods instead. For example, measuring the height of a tall building might involve calculating based on shadow length and angle, rather than physically measuring the structure itself.

**Instrumental Measurement**
The development of specialized instruments has revolutionized measuring capabilities. From simple thermometers to sophisticated spectrometers, these tools extend human sensory capabilities and allow for measurements of extraordinary precision.

## The Role of Standardization

Regardless of the specific method employed, standardization remains crucial. Without agreed-upon units and consistent methodology, measurements become meaningless for comparison or communication purposes. The International System of Units (SI) represents humanity's effort to create universal standards that enable consistent measuring across different contexts and cultures.

## Conclusion

Understanding the appropriate method for measuring any given phenomenon is essential for obtaining meaningful, accurate results. As technology advances, measuring methods continue to evolve, offering greater precision and enabling us to quantify aspects of our world that were previously immeasurable.

## Method for Measuring and Reporting Uplink and Downlink Packet Transmission Latency in a Cellular Network

### Field of Invention
This invention relates to wireless communication systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for measuring, computing, and reporting packet transmission latency for both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) data flows between a User Equipment (UE) and a network entity in a cellular network.

---

### Claim 1 (Independent Method Claim)

A method performed by a network entity for measuring and reporting packet transmission latency in a cellular network, the method comprising:

1. **Configuring** a User Equipment (UE) with latency measurement parameters, including at least one Quality of Service (QoS) flow identifier, a measurement periodicity, and a reporting trigger condition;

2. **Receiving**, from the UE, a first timestamp associated with a first data packet transmitted in an uplink direction, the first timestamp indicating a time of transmission from the UE;

3. **Recording**, at the network entity, a second timestamp indicating a time of reception of the first data packet at the network entity;

4. **Computing** an uplink latency value based on a difference between the second timestamp and the first timestamp;

5. **Recording**, at the network entity, a third timestamp indicating a time of transmission of a second data packet from the network entity to the UE in a downlink direction;

6. **Receiving**, from the UE, a fourth timestamp indicating a time of reception of the second data packet at the UE;

7. **Computing** a downlink latency value based on a difference between the fourth timestamp and the third timestamp;

8. **Generating** a latency report comprising the uplink latency value, the downlink latency value, and an identifier corresponding to the QoS flow or bearer associated with the measured packets; and

9. **Transmitting** the latency report to a network management function or an application function for at least one of network optimization, Service Level Agreement (SLA) verification, or QoS adjustment.

---

### Claim 2 (Dependent Claim – UE-side Reporting)

The method of Claim 1, wherein the UE reports the fourth timestamp using a Radio Resource Control (RRC) message or a Medium Access Control (MAC) control element, and wherein the reporting is triggered upon at least one of:
(a) expiration of the measurement periodicity;
(b) the latency value exceeding a configured threshold; or
(c) receipt of an explicit polling request from the network entity.

---

### Claim 3 (Dependent Claim – Synchronization)

The method of Claim 1, further comprising synchronizing a clock of the UE with a clock of the network entity using a reference timing signal, wherein the first, second, third, and fourth timestamps are derived based on the synchronized clock to ensure timestamp accuracy within a predetermined tolerance.

---

### Claim 4 (Dependent Claim – Aggregated Reporting)

The method of Claim 1, wherein the latency report further comprises statistical latency metrics selected from the group consisting of: average latency, maximum latency, minimum latency, latency variance (jitter), and a percentile-based latency value, computed over a plurality of uplink and downlink packets within the measurement periodicity.

---

### Claim 5 (Dependent Claim – Differentiated QoS Flows)

The method of Claim 1, wherein the UE is configured with a plurality of QoS flow identifiers corresponding to a plurality of data flows having different QoS requirements, and wherein the latency report includes separate uplink and downlink latency values for each of the plurality of QoS flows.

---

### Claim 6 (Independent Apparatus Claim – Network Entity)

A network entity in a cellular network, comprising:
- a transceiver configured to communicate with a User Equipment (UE);
- a memory storing instructions; and
- a processor configured to execute the instructions to perform the method of any one of Claims 1 to 5.

---

### Claim 7 (Independent Apparatus Claim – UE)

A User Equipment (UE) in a cellular network, comprising:

- a memory storing instructions; and
- a processor configured to execute the instructions to:
  - generate and transmit a first timestamp associated with an uplink data packet;
  - receive a downlink data packet and record a corresponding reception timestamp;

### Claim 8 (Dependent Claim – Non-Transitory Computer-Readable Medium)

# Timestamp-Based Latency Measurement in Wireless UL/DL Communication

## Overview

This method enables precise measurement of transmission latency in wireless networks by embedding timestamps directly into uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) packet headers or payloads. By comparing timestamps at transmission and reception points, the system calculates one-way or round-trip latency without requiring dedicated test traffic.

## System Architecture

### Participants
- **User Equipment (UE)**: Transmits UL packets, receives DL packets
- **Base Station / Access Point (BS/AP)**: Receives UL packets, transmits DL packets
- **Synchronization Reference**: Common time source (e.g., GPS, PTP grandmaster, or network time protocol) ensuring both endpoints share a synchronized clock domain

### Timestamp Insertion Points
Timestamps are embedded at the **MAC layer** or **PHY layer** framing stage, capturing the time as close as possible to actual radio transmission (to minimize software/stack-induced jitter).

## Packet Structure

Each UL/DL packet includes a **Timestamp Field (TS)**, typically appended to the header:

```
| Preamble | MAC Header | TS_tx (e.g., 32/64-bit) | Payload | FCS/CRC |
```

- **TS_tx**: Time of transmission, sampled from the local hardware clock immediately before/during radio-frontend handoff
- Resolution: nanosecond to microsecond granularity, depending on clock source (e.g., PPS-disciplined oscillators)

## Latency Calculation Procedure

### 1. One-Way Latency (Requires Synchronized Clocks)

**Downlink example:**
1. BS embeds `TS_tx_DL` at the moment of transmission
2. UE records `TS_rx_DL` upon successful packet reception (post-demodulation, pre-processing)
3. Latency is computed as:

```
Latency_DL = TS_rx_DL - TS_tx_DL
```

**Uplink example (symmetric):**
```
Latency_UL = TS_rx_UL - TS_tx_UL
```

This approach requires tight time synchronization between UE and BS clocks (sub-microsecond accuracy), often achieved via:
- IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP)
- GPS-disciplined oscillators
- Air-interface synchronization signals (e.g., 5G NR SSB timing)

### 2. Round-Trip Time (RTT) — Clock-Synchronization-Independent

For systems lacking synchronized clocks, RTT avoids absolute clock alignment errors:

1. UE transmits UL packet with `TS_tx_UL`
2. BS receives at `TS_rx_UL`, immediately triggers a DL response containing:
   - Original `TS_tx_UL` (echoed back)
   - New `TS_tx_DL` (BS's own transmission time)
3. UE receives DL packet at `TS_rx_DL`
4. UE calculates:

```
RTT = (TS_rx_DL - TS_tx_UL) - (TS_tx_DL - TS_rx_UL)
```

The term `(TS_tx_DL - TS_rx_UL)` represents the **processing/turnaround delay** at the BS, which is subtracted to isolate pure propagation + queuing latency.

One-way latency (approximate, assuming symmetric UL/DL paths):
```
Latency ≈ RTT / 2
```

## Key Design Considerations

### Clock Synchronization Accuracy
- Timestamp resolution must be finer than the latency being measured
- Clock drift between measurement intervals must be bounded or periodically recalibrated
- Asymmetric propagation delays (common in FDD systems) introduce error in the RTT/2 approximation

### Timestamp Insertion Timing
- **Ideal**: Timestamp captured at the antenna reference point (post-PHY encoding)
- **Practical**: Often captured at MAC-PHY interface, introducing a small, deterministic offset that can be calibrated out

### Packet Overhead
- Additional bits for TS field increase overhead; tradeoff between timestamp resolution (bit-width) and payload efficiency
- Can be mitigated by embedding timestamps only in periodic control/reference packets rather than every data packet

### Multi-Hop / Relay Scenarios
- Each hop appends or updates timestamp fields, allowing per-hop latency decomposition
- Cumulative latency calculated by summing hop-wise `(TS_rx - TS_tx)` differences

## Example Use Cases
- **5G URLLC** (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication) validation and SLA monitoring
- **Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)** over wireless bridges
- **Industrial IoT** control loops requiring deterministic latency bounds
- **Network diagnostics** for identifying congestion or scheduling-induced delay spikes

## Error Sources and Mitigation

| Error Source | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Clock drift | Periodic re-synchronization (e.g., every N packets) |
| Quantization error (timestamp resolution) | Use higher-resolution counters (≥10 ns granularity) |
| Processing jitter at insertion/extraction | Hardware-based timestamping (NIC/PHY-level) instead of software timestamps |
| Asymmetric UL/DL delay | Separate one-way calibration using synchronized clocks where possible |

---

This timestamp-embedding approach provides fine-grained, in-band latency measurement suitable for real-time network performance monitoring and closed-loop latency optimization in modern wireless systems.

# Invention Disclosure

## Title
**Method and Apparatus for Measuring Packet Latency Between a User Equipment (UE) and Network Entity Using Timestamp-Based Techniques**

---

## 1. Field of the Invention

This invention relates to wireless communication systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for measuring, reporting, and utilizing end-to-end or one-way packet latency between a User Equipment (UE) and a network entity (e.g., gNB, base station, or core network function) using send-time and receive-time timestamps.

---

## 2. Background / Problem Statement

Modern wireless networks (5G, 6G, and beyond) increasingly support latency-sensitive applications such as Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC), extended reality (XR), industrial automation, and time-sensitive networking (TSN). Accurate, real-time measurement of packet latency is critical for:

- Quality of Service (QoS) enforcement and adaptation
- Network slicing performance validation
- Radio resource scheduling optimization
- Root-cause analysis of latency violations
- Service Level Agreement (SLA) monitoring

Existing latency estimation techniques often rely on indirect measurements (e.g., RTT approximations, statistical inference from buffer states) that lack precision, or require external protocols (e.g., NTP/PTP-based probes) that are not tightly integrated with the air-interface protocol stack. There is a need for a lightweight, protocol-integrated mechanism that allows a UE and network entity to directly and accurately measure one-way or round-trip packet latency using embedded timestamps, without requiring external timing infrastructure.

---

## 3. Summary of the Invention

The invention provides a method and system wherein:

1. A **sending entity** (UE or network entity) inserts a **send timestamp (T1)** into a packet, protocol data unit (PDU), or associated control message at the time of transmission.
2. A **receiving entity** records a **receive timestamp (T2)** upon reception of the packet.
3. The latency is computed as:
   
   **Latency = T2 − T1** (one-way), or
   
   **RTT = (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2)** (round-trip, if a response packet is used), where T3 and T4 are the send and receive timestamps of the response.

4. The computed latency value is used for:
   - Local QoS monitoring and reporting to the network (e.g., via RRC, MAC-CE, or a new control PDU)
   - Triggering adaptive actions (e.g., scheduling changes, modulation/coding scheme adjustment, handover decisions)
   - Network-side analytics and SLA verification

5. Optional **clock synchronization compensation** is applied using a reference synchronization mechanism (e.g., 5G-based timing reference, GPS-disciplined clock, or PTP) to correct for clock offset between UE and network entity when computing one-way latency.

---

## 4. Detailed Description

### 4.1 System Architecture

The system comprises:
- **UE**: Equipped with a local clock, timestamping module, and latency computation/reporting logic.
- **Network Entity** (e.g., gNB, UPF, or edge server): Equipped with a synchronized or independent local clock, timestamping module, and latency aggregation/reporting logic.
- **Optional Time Synchronization Reference**: A common reference clock source (e.g., GNSS, PTP grandmaster) to align UE and network clocks for one-way latency accuracy.

### 4.2 Timestamp Insertion

- The sending entity generates timestamp **T1** at the moment of packet transmission (e.g., at PDCP, RLC, or application layer boundary).
- T1 is embedded into:
  - A dedicated field in a new or existing control PDU (e.g., MAC Control Element, RRC message, or PDCP header extension), or
  - A payload-level timestamp field (e.g., in a GTP-U header extension for network-side measurement).

### 4.3 Timestamp Capture at Reception

- Upon receiving the packet, the receiving entity captures **T2** using its local clock, ideally at the earliest possible protocol layer (e.g., PHY/MAC boundary) to minimize measurement jitter from internal processing.

### 4.4 Latency Computation

- **One-Way Latency**: Computed directly as T2 − T1, assuming synchronized clocks. Clock offset correction may be applied:
  
  Latency_corrected = (T2 − T1) − ClockOffset

- **Round-Trip Latency**: Computed using a four-timestamp exchange (T1, T2, T3, T4) to eliminate the need for clock synchronization:

  RTT = (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2)

  This method is particularly advantageous when UE and network clocks are not synchronized, as clock offset cancels out in the RTT formula.

### 4.5 Reporting Mechanism

- The measured latency (or raw timestamps) is reported via:
  - New or existing RRC signaling (for UE-initiated reporting)
  - MAC-CE (for low-latency, frequent reporting)
  - Application-layer QoS reports
  - New GTP-U/N3 interface extensions (for network-internal latency measurement, e.g., UPF-to-gNB)

- Reporting may be:
  - **Periodic**: at configured intervals
  - **Event-triggered**: when latency exceeds a configured threshold
  - **On-demand**: upon network request

### 4.6 Use Cases

1. **QoS Flow Monitoring**: Latency measurements per QoS flow to verify compliance with 5QI/QoS profile requirements.
2. **Dynamic Scheduling Adaptation**: gNB adjusts scheduling priority based on observed latency trends.
3. **Network Slicing SLA Verification**: Latency statistics aggregated per slice for SLA compliance reporting.
4. **Handover/Mobility Optimization**: Latency spikes used as a trigger for proactive handover decisions.
5. **URLLC/TSN Applications**: Fine-grained latency measurement supports deterministic networking requirements.

---

## 5. Example Signaling Flow

```
UE                                Network Entity (gNB/UPF)
 |                                        |
 |--- Packet with Timestamp T1 --------->|
 |                                        | Capture T2
 |                                        |
 |<--- Response with T3, T2 -------------|
 | Capture T4                            |
 |                                        |
 | Compute RTT = (T4-T1) - (T3-T2)       |
 |                                        |
 |--- Latency Report (RRC/MAC-CE) ------>|
```

---

## 6. Novel Aspects / Claims Focus

1. **Embedding send/receive timestamps within air-interface protocol layers** (e.g., MAC-CE, PDCP header extension) rather than relying solely on application-layer or external protocol timestamping.
2. **Dual-mode latency computation** supporting both one-way (synchronized clock) and round-trip (clock-offset-independent) measurement using a unified signaling framework.
3. **Adaptive, event-triggered latency reporting** integrated with existing RRC/MAC signaling to minimize overhead while maintaining measurement granularity.
4. **Cross-layer latency measurement** spanning UE, RAN, and core network (e.g., UPF) using consistent timestamp semantics across interfaces (Uu, N3, F1).
5. Use of measured latency as **direct input to scheduler, handover, and QoS enforcement algorithms** in real time (closed-loop latency-aware control).

---

## 7. Advantages Over Prior Art

| Aspect | Prior Art | This Invention |
|---|---|---|
| Measurement method | Indirect (RTT estimation, buffer inference) | Direct timestamp-based measurement |
| Synchronization dependency | Often requires external PTP/NTP | Optional; RTT mode works without sync |
| Integration | External probes/application-layer only | Integrated into air-interface protocol stack |
| Granularity | Coarse, periodic | Fine-grained, per-packet or per-flow |
| Reporting overhead | High (separate protocol) | Low (reuses existing signaling, e.g., MAC-CE) |

---

## 8. Alternative Embodiments

1. Timestamps may be inserted at multiple protocol layers simultaneously (e.g., PHY, MAC, PDCP) to isolate latency contribution per layer.
2. Timestamp fields may use compressed/relative encoding (e.g., delta from a reference epoch) to reduce signaling overhead.
3. Latency measurements may be aggregated and reported as statistical summaries (min/max/average/jitter) rather than raw timestamps.
4. The invention may be extended to **multi-hop latency measurement** (e.g., UE-gNB-UPF-Application Server) using timestamp propagation across multiple entities.
5. Machine learning models may consume historical latency measurements to **predict future latency** and proactively adjust network parameters.

---

## 9. Potential Claims (Draft)

**Claim 1:** A method performed by a user equipment (UE) comprising: generating a first timestamp corresponding to a transmission time of a packet; transmitting the packet including the first timestamp to a network entity; and receiving, from the network entity, an indication of a second timestamp corresponding to a reception time of the packet by the network entity, wherein a latency value is derived based on the first timestamp and the second timestamp.

**Claim 2:** The method of claim 1, wherein the first timestamp and the second timestamp are used to compute a round-trip time based on a third timestamp corresponding to a transmission time of a response packet from the network entity and a fourth timestamp corresponding to a reception time of the response packet at the UE.

**Claim 3:** The method of claim 1, wherein the first timestamp is embedded within a Medium Access Control Control Element (MAC-CE).

**Claim 4:** A network entity configured to: receive a packet from a UE, the packet including a first timestamp corresponding to a transmission time at the UE; generate a second timestamp corresponding to a reception time of the packet; and transmit a latency-related report based on the first timestamp and the second timestamp.

**Claim 5:** The method of claim 1, further comprising adjusting a scheduling parameter based on the derived latency value.

counterfactuals.output:
# Latency Measurement in 5G Networks Using Timing-Tagged Packets

## Overview

This method leverages timestamp information embedded in both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) packets to enable precise, bidirectional latency measurement within the 5G system, often used for Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication) applications, and QoS monitoring.

## Core Mechanism

### 1. **Timestamp Insertion**
- When a packet is generated (e.g., by a UE or a network function like the UPF/gNB), a **timestamp (T1)** is inserted into the packet header or a dedicated control field.
- This can occur at multiple points in the protocol stack (PDCP, SDAP, or application layer) depending on implementation.

### 2. **Bidirectional Tagging**
- **Downlink (DL) packets**: The network (e.g., UPF or gNB) inserts a timestamp when the packet is sent toward the UE.
- **Uplink (UL) packets**: The UE inserts a timestamp when it sends a packet back toward the network.
- Optionally, the UE or network can **echo back** the received DL timestamp in its next UL packet (or vice versa), similar to a ping-pong mechanism.

### 3. **Delay Calculation**
At the receiving end, the entity compares:
- **T1** (timestamp when packet was sent)
- **T2** (timestamp when packet was received)

$$\text{One-way delay} = T2 - T1$$

For round-trip measurement:
$$\text{RTT} = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2)$$

Where:
- T1 = UE sends UL packet
- T2 = Network receives UL packet
- T3 = Network sends DL response
- T4 = UE receives DL response

This is similar to the NTP/PTP (Precision Time Protocol) delay computation model.

## Architectural Placement (5G System)

```
UE ──────── gNB ──────── UPF ──────── Application Server
 |            |            |                |
 T1 (UL)    Relay        T2 (UL rx)      
 T4 (DL rx) Relay        T3 (DL tx)
```

- **UE side**: Application or modem stack inserts/reads timestamps.
- **gNB side**: May relay or add its own processing delay markers (for RAN-only latency).
- **UPF side**: Often the reference point for **PDU session-level latency** (per 3GPP TS 23.501/29.244).

## Triggering Actions Based on Delay

Once delay (D) is computed, the system compares it against a **threshold (D_th)**:

```
If D > D_th:
    Trigger action (e.g.):
        - QoS flow re-negotiation
        - Handover trigger
        - Switch to redundant path (URLLC dual connectivity)
        - Adjust scheduling priority
        - Alert network management system (via NWDAF)
Else:
    Continue normal operation
```

## Standard-Aligned Techniques

| Mechanism | Description |
|---|---|
| **GTP-U Extension Headers** | Can carry timestamps in UL/DL GTP-U packets between gNB and UPF |
| **PDCP/RLC timestamps** | Used for RAN-level latency tracking |
| **5G QoS Monitoring (TS 28.552 / TS 23.501)** | Defines "QoS Monitoring for URLLC" using DL/UL packet delay measurement |
| **NWDAF (Network Data Analytics Function)** | Collects delay statistics, feeds into automation loops |
| **TSN integration (IEEE 802.1AS + 5GS)** | Uses gPTP timestamps carried transparently through 5G as a TSN bridge |

## Example: 3GPP QoS Monitoring for URLLC (TS 23.501 Annex)

1. UPF inserts DL packet delay timestamp in GTP-U header extension.
2. RAN (gNB) forwards this along with its own reception time.
3. UE (or RAN) computes DL packet delay.
4. Similarly, UE inserts UL timestamp; UPF computes UL delay upon reception.
5. Combined UL+DL delay gives **PDU session round-trip latency**.
6. If delay exceeds SLA threshold → **PCF/SMF notified** → may adjust:
   - QoS Flow parameters
   - Trigger UPF relocation (edge computing move closer to UE)
   - Trigger network slicing reconfiguration

## Key Benefits

- **No need for external synchronized clocks** if using round-trip (ping-pong) style calculation.
- **Real-time triggering** enables **closed-loop automation** (e.g., SLA enforcement, dynamic slicing).
- Supports **both RAN-level and end-to-end (UPF-to-UE) latency** measurement.

## Summary

This method — often called **timestamp-based two-way delay measurement** — embeds send/receive timestamps in UL and DL packets, computes one-way or round-trip delay by comparing these timestamps, and uses the computed delay against a threshold to trigger network actions such as QoS adjustment, handover, or slice reconfiguration. It's foundational to 5G's support for **URLLC** and **TSN integration**, and is standardized partially under **3GPP's QoS monitoring framework** (TS 23.501, TS 28.552).

# PATENT CLAIM LANGUAGE
## Process for Reporting Packet Transmission Delay Based on Timestamp Comparison

---

### CLAIM 1 (Independent Method Claim)

A method for reporting packet transmission delay between a user equipment (UE) and a network entity, the method comprising:

receiving, at the UE, a data packet from the network entity, wherein the data packet comprises a first timestamp indicating a time at which the data packet was transmitted by the network entity;

generating, at the UE, a second timestamp indicating a time at which the data packet was received by the UE;

calculating, at the UE, a transmission delay value based on a difference between the second timestamp and the first timestamp;

generating a delay report comprising the calculated transmission delay value; and

transmitting, from the UE to the network entity, the delay report,

wherein the delay report is configured to enable the network entity to adjust one or more transmission parameters based on the calculated transmission delay value.

---

### CLAIM 2 (Dependent Claim - Synchronization)

The method of claim 1, further comprising:

synchronizing a clock of the UE with a clock of the network entity prior to receiving the data packet, wherein the synchronizing comprises exchanging one or more reference timing signals between the UE and the network entity to establish a common time reference for generating the first timestamp and the second timestamp.

---

### CLAIM 3 (Dependent Claim - Threshold-Based Reporting)

The method of claim 1, wherein transmitting the delay report to the network entity comprises:

comparing the calculated transmission delay value to a predetermined delay threshold; and

transmitting the delay report only in response to determining that the calculated transmission delay value exceeds the predetermined delay threshold.

---

### CLAIM 4 (Dependent Claim - Periodic Reporting)

The method of claim 1, wherein transmitting the delay report to the network entity comprises:

accumulating a plurality of transmission delay values over a predetermined time interval;

computing a statistical metric based on the plurality of transmission delay values, wherein the statistical metric comprises at least one of an average delay, a maximum delay, a minimum delay, or a delay variance; and

transmitting the delay report comprising the statistical metric to the network entity upon expiration of the predetermined time interval.

---

### CLAIM 5 (Dependent Claim - Packet Identification)

The method of claim 1, wherein the data packet further comprises a packet sequence identifier, and wherein the delay report further comprises the packet sequence identifier associated with the calculated transmission delay value.

---

### CLAIM 6 (Independent Method Claim - Network Entity Perspective)

A method for adjusting network transmission parameters based on reported packet delay, the method comprising:

transmitting, from a network entity to a user equipment (UE), a data packet comprising a first timestamp indicating a transmission time of the data packet;

receiving, at the network entity from the UE, a delay report comprising a transmission delay value, wherein the transmission delay value is calculated based on a difference between a second timestamp indicating a reception time of the data packet at the UE and the first timestamp;

determining, based on the transmission delay value, whether the transmission delay value satisfies a predetermined criterion; and

adjusting, in response to determining that the transmission delay value satisfies the predetermined criterion, at least one transmission parameter selected from the group consisting of: a modulation and coding scheme, a scheduling priority, a transmission power level, and a resource allocation.

---

### CLAIM 7 (Independent Apparatus Claim - UE)

A user equipment (UE) configured for reporting packet transmission delay, the UE comprising:

a transceiver configured to receive a data packet from a network entity, the data packet comprising a first timestamp indicating a transmission time of the data packet;

a processor operatively coupled to the transceiver; and

a memory storing instructions that, when executed by the processor, cause the UE to:
- generate a second timestamp indicating a reception time of the data packet at the UE;
- calculate a transmission delay value based on a difference between the second timestamp and the first timestamp;
- generate a delay report comprising the transmission delay value; and
- transmit, via the transceiver, the delay report to the network entity.

---

### CLAIM 8 (Independent Apparatus Claim - Network Entity)

A network entity configured for adjusting transmission parameters based on reported packet delay, the network entity comprising:

a transceiver configured to transmit a data packet to a user equipment (UE) and receive a delay report from the UE, the data packet comprising a first timestamp, and the delay report comprising a transmission delay value calculated based on a difference between a second timestamp generated at the UE and the first timestamp;

a processor operatively coupled to the transceiver; and

a memory storing instructions that, when executed by the processor, cause the network entity to:
- evaluate the transmission delay value against a predetermined threshold; and
- adjust at least one transmission parameter in response to the transmission delay value exceeding the predetermined threshold.

---

### CLAIM 9 (Dependent Claim - Non-Transitory Computer Readable Medium)

A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors of a user equipment (UE), cause the UE to perform the method of claim 1.

---

### CLAIM 10 (Dependent Claim - Encoding Format)

The method of claim 1, wherein the first timestamp and the second timestamp are encoded according to a common time format comprising at least one of: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), GPS time, or a network-specific reference clock format synchronized via a Precision Time Protocol (PTP).

---

*[End of Claim Set]*

---

**Note:** This claim language is a drafting template/example for illustrative purposes. Actual patent claims should be prepared and reviewed by a registered patent attorney or agent to ensure proper claim scope, support in the specification, and compliance with applicable patent office rules (e.g., USPTO, EPO).
